# Feasibility report — improving a local 2B MT model with context, disambiguation, retrieval, refinement, reranking, and selective review

Executive summary
Document/context-aware methods, targeted sense‑disambiguation signals, glossary retrieval, PEFT/quantized fine‑tuning, n‑best generation + reranking, and confidence‑triggered fallback are individually supported by reproducible research; combining them on a small local 2B model is feasible and cost‑effective in many realistic deployment profiles but requires careful tradeoffs between quality gains, latency/memory, and safety risks (data contamination, privacy leakage, and hallucination amplification). Quantitative gains vary by language pair, metric, and method; resource costs are dominated by (a) reranker/evaluator compute for n‑best selection, (b) retrieval index size and reranking throughput, and (c) fine‑tuning GPU hours when full‑model updates are performed. The evidence below cites primary papers and repos and separates measured results from design proposals or conceptual recommendations. [1], [4], [20], [17], [18]

Feasibility and measured gains (synthesis)
- Document‑level context: multiple document‑aware NMT architectures produce consistent BLEU/chrF gains over sentence models; reported gains in controlled experiments range from modest (~0.9 BLEU) to larger depending on selection/representation of context and dataset, with significant language‑pair variability (examples include English↔German and TED/IWSLT benchmarks). These are measured, reproducible improvements in peer‑reviewed work. [1], [4], [5]

- Sense disambiguation (explicit signals or prompting): evaluated prompting/“predicted sense” approaches with 1–3 shot LLM setups show measurable ChrF++ gains (~0.7–1.8 chrF++ points on narrow sense benchmarks) and outperform naïve “all senses” prompts; this suggests explicit disambiguation signals can yield small but reliable lexical improvements for ambiguous items. (These results are measured on the reported NLS/TS evaluations and specific LLMs.) [2]

- Retrieval of translator‑approved terminology: retrieval‑augmented localization (RAL) improved MQM scores and reduced terminology errors substantially (terminology errors down by ~16–45% across languages), and brought an open LLM’s MQM close to top providers in the reported experiments — showing strong, measured benefit of runtime glossary retrieval. [3]

- Source‑grounded refinement (fine‑tuning / self‑training / selective back‑translation): high‑quality fine‑tuning recipes (two‑stage monolingual then small high‑quality parallel data) produced large BLEU/COMET gains in LLM translation studies; classical back‑translation / self‑training improves low‑resource performance when used carefully, and MBR‑selected self‑training can improve validation results in recent work. Fine‑tuning costs vary sharply: small‑model PEFT is cheap, but full fine‑tuning (or large model training) requires substantial GPU‑hours reported in experimental papers. [13], [14], [15], [16], [18]

- n‑best generation and reranking: reranking with learned/evaluation metrics (DrNMT, COMET‑MBR) produces measurable gains (e.g., higher COMET and sometimes BLEU/chrF improvements in WMT systems), but computational cost grows with candidate count and scorer complexity; efficient pipelines prune candidates before heavy scoring. Reranking effectiveness improves with larger candidate sets and stronger scorers but requires extra compute for scoring (O(N × cost_of_metric)). [10], [11], [12]

- Selective review / fallback to a stronger model: quality‑estimation pipelines and confidence filtering reduce post‑editing effort by routing low‑confidence segments to human post‑editors or stronger models; open frameworks and empirical work support QE‑based triage but caution that QE models themselves may mispredict without careful calibration. [16], [27]

Resource and deployment implications (three representative profiles)
- CPU‑only desktop: document/context encoders, simple glossary injection via lexically constrained decoding, and offline retrieval using a small on‑disk BM25/FAISS hybrid (chunk sizes 300–500 tokens) are feasible; large reranking or on‑device PEFT should be avoided due to latency and RAM limits. (Indexing/storage tradeoffs: FAISS guidance and vector‑storage size estimates are available for planning.) [9], [8], [30]

- Consumer GPU (~8–16 GB VRAM): quantized 4‑ or 8‑bit inference plus LoRA/QLoRA-style adapters is supported by community tooling (BitsAndBytes, QLoRA recipes) and fits typical 8–16 GB cards for 2–7B models when using 4‑bit and adapter approaches; measured inference frameworks (CTranslate2) show multi‑k tokens/sec throughput with modest GPU memory. PEFT (LoRA ranks 8–16) and 4‑bit quantization are reproducible choices for a 2B model, but papers report QLoRA experiments primarily on ≥2.7B models — applicability to 2B is plausible but not explicitly measured in the cited evidence. [22], [19], [20], [21], [17]

- Larger workstation GPU (≥24 GB): supports more aggressive PEFT/fine‑tuning, larger retriever indices in RAM, and on‑the‑fly reranking with learned scorers; measured GPU‑hour figures for RAG fine‑tuning across models illustrate how costs scale with model size and training epochs. [18]

Costs vs. measured gains (high‑level)
- Quality gains are generally incremental per technique (document context and good fine‑tuning yield the largest measured BLEU/COMET improvements; explicit sense prompting and glossary retrieval yield smaller but high‑precision lexical/terminology improvements). Reranking and QE bring robust COMET/MQM improvements in shared tasks but consume additional CPU/GPU per segment. Training/fine‑tuning costs are reported in GPU‑hours and can be significant for larger models; PEFT/QLoRA reduces GPU memory and training cost substantially. [1], [2], [3], [10], [13], [18], [20]

Concrete risks and mitigations
- Data contamination / privacy leakage: DP‑SGD or applying differential privacy only to fine‑tuned layers can bound leakage but imposes 3–5× training overhead; freezing base layers and using LoRA reduces DP cost. Evidence supports applying DP cautiously and only where required. [23], [19]

- Hallucination amplification via self‑refinement/back‑translation: self‑training and back‑translation help low‑resource cases but can amplify model errors if synthetic data is noisy; mitigation includes MBR selection of synthetic pairs, manual sampling, and post‑filtering. Recent guidance emphasizes selection and validation of synthetic data. [14], [15], [16], [24]

- QE / confidence errors: QE models can misclassify; use ensembles, calibration, and human review thresholds; OpenKiwi and related frameworks are available for developing and validating QE models. [16], [27]

Recommended experimental protocol (concise)
- Benchmarks: evaluate on document‑level IWSLT/WMT subsets, FLORES‑101 for multilingual coverage, MuCoW or targeted WSD suites for sense tests, and an MQM human evaluation for high‑value segments. [4], [11], [5]

- PEFT & quantization: try LoRA ranks r=8 and r=16; evaluate QLoRA (4‑bit) adapters where supported (note: some QLoRA experiments are reported for ≥2.7B models). Use BitsAndBytes for 4‑bit inference and CTranslate2 for high‑throughput baselines. [20], [19], [22], [17]

- Glossary injection: implement lexically constrained decoding or soft‑constrained augmentation (use O(1) constrained decoding implementations where available) and runtime retrieval (BM25+FAISS hybrid, chunk 300–500 tokens) with reranking over retrieved passages. [29], [8], [9]

- Reranking & QE: generate n≈8–32 candidates, prune with a cheap scorer, then rerank with COMET or learned QE/reward model; measure O(N×cost) tradeoffs and tune candidate count vs latency. [12], [10], [11]

MQM professional evaluation setup
- Use trained MQM experts; adopt MQM taxonomy (Accuracy, Fluency, Terminology, Style, Locale, etc.) with flat severity penalties (Major −5, Minor −1, Neutral 0) and annotate a stratified sample (suggest pilot 200–400 segments per system to estimate effect sizes; evidence notes MQM is costly and requires experts). Calibrate annotators, compute inter‑annotator agreement, and report MQM scores with confidence intervals. The literature highlights MQM’s cost and expert requirement compared with DA/SQM. [26], [25], [27]

Prioritized reading / repositories (by technique)
- Document context: thesis and MDPI survey [1], [4]
- Sense disambiguation (measured): LORESLM paper [2] and WSD methods [6], repository example [7]
- Retrieval & glossaries: RAL study and FAISS guidance [3], [8]; retriever design notes [9]
- Reranking: IJCNLP and WMT system writeups (DrNMT, COMET‑MBR) [10], [11], plus reranking complexity analysis [12]
- PEFT/quantization: QLoRA reports and practical guides [20], [19], [21], [22]
- Self‑training/back‑translation: classical and recent works [14], [15], [16]
- Inference toolbenchmarks: CTranslate2 repo for throughput/memory baselines [17]
- Privacy: DP guidance for fine‑tuning [23]
- MQM / human evaluation: MQM annotation guidance and sampling notes [26], [25], [27]

Evidence gaps
- No direct, single paper measures the full integrated stack (document context + explicit WSD module + glossary retrieval + QLoRA fine‑tuning + n‑best reranking + QE fallback) on a 2B local model; most studies evaluate subsets. Reported QLoRA results focus on ≥2.7B models, so direct measured memory/perf numbers for QLoRA on 2B are not specified in the findings. [20], [18]
